text: A robot moves only right or down, from the top-left of a grid to the bottom-right — but now some cells are obstacles, marked one, and can't be entered. Return the number of unique paths.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — a path can't pass through any obstacle, and if the start or end is an obstacle, the answer is zero?
Exactly. Grid up to a hundred by a hundred, and the answer fits in a thirty-two-bit int.
Let me run through an example. A three by three grid with the center blocked has two paths — one hugs the top-right, one the bottom-left.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. This problem reminds me of a two-D grid DP for counting paths, with one extra rule. Same recurrence — dp of i, j is the cell above plus the cell to the left — but an obstacle cell gets dp zero. I can't stand on it, so it contributes zero to its right and down neighbors, and paths route around it. The combinatorial choose formula no longer applies once there are obstacles, so DP is the way.

Here's the plan. One: if the start or end is an obstacle, return zero. Two: seed the start with one. Three: for each cell, an obstacle stays zero, otherwise add the cell above and the cell to the left; return the bottom-right. One thing worth flagging — the first row and column are not all one here: once an edge hits an obstacle, everything after it is zero, because the straight corridor is cut. A padded m plus one by n plus one grid of zeros lets the first real row and column use the same formula, with no boundary special-casing. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. Code the padded version and an order n space one.

The padded two-D version: the extra border of zeros is a sentinel, and real cell i minus one, j minus one lives at dp i, j. And an order n space rolling version that reuses one row. Both are order m times n time. One thing worth flagging — in the padded version, the update adds onto dp of i, j itself instead of overwriting it. That's what keeps the seed: at the start, up and left are both sentinel zeros, so a plain assignment would wipe the one. And in the rolling version, an obstacle must set dp of j to zero explicitly; it still carries last row's value, so skipping it would wrongly treat the cell as passable.

Let's dry-run the three by three with the center blocked — expected two. The center stays zero, so it feeds its neighbors nothing, and the corner is up one plus left one, two. Correct. Edge cases: a blocked start gives zero, and a full obstacle row across the middle gives zero. A single open cell gives one.

Time is order m times n, space order m times n, or order n with the rolling row. Oh, one more thing — the whole change from the plain grid-path count is one line: obstacle means zero. The padding trick removes the first row and column special cases, and the closed-form combinatorics dies here because obstacles break the assumption that every down-right sequence is a valid path. Swap the plus for a min and set obstacles to infinity, and it becomes a minimum-cost path with walls.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You saw it's the basic path count plus obstacle equals zero, and that edges after an obstacle go to zero. You used padding to kill the boundary cases, and knew the rolling version must clear dp of j. And you explained why the combinatorial formula no longer works. Good work.
